claim.pdf_says: In 8.8.1.5.4 the cases 'a)' through 'd)' are indented one level under item '2) When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero, the results shall be determined as follows:'.
claim.markdown_says:
2) When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero, the results shall be determined as follows:

a) When operand-2 is an integer and the following condition is true
...
d) When operand-2 is an integer and the following condition is true   (a)-d) written flush left, at the same indentation as 1) and 2))
claim.why_it_matters: The a)-d) cases are conditional on item 2); flattening them to the outer margin loses the nesting that scopes them, the same convention page 208 and page 213 observe with three-space indentation.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED - this is leading-whitespace formatting, not a content discrepancy. (1) Both observations of fact are correct. The 300dpi render of PDF page 211 (printed 181) shows '1)' and '2)' at the left text margin and 'a)' through 'd)' indented one level, with their sub-content ('(operand-2 = 1)', 'the equivalent expression shall be', '(operand-1)', etc.) indented further; specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 9174-9210 write every one of those lines at column 0. (2) But NOTHING is missing, reordered, or altered. Every item and every display expression is present verbatim and in correct sequence: '(1)' (L9176); a) '(operand-2 = 1)' / 'the equivalent expression shall be' / '(operand-1)' (L9180-9186); b) '(operand-2 = 2)' / '(operand-1 * operand-1)' (L9188-9194); c) '(operand-2 = 3)' / '((operand-1 * operand-1) * operand-1)' (L9196-9202); d) '(operand-2 = 4)' / '((operand-1 * operand-1) * (operand-1 * operand-1))' (L9204-9210). (3) I read the printed enumerator glyphs directly: the PDF prints '1)', '2)', then 'a)', 'b)', 'c)', 'd)' with closing parentheses, and the markdown reproduces exactly those six enumerators. No enumerator is lost or changed. The nesting is therefore still carried unambiguously by the enumerator SERIES itself - a lowercase-letter list cannot be read as continuing an Arabic-numeral list, so no reader or downstream consumer can mistake 'a)' for a peer of '1)' and '2)'. Meaning is fully preserved. (4) The three-space indentation the claim holds up as the lost convention is not semantic markup even where it appears: CommonMark strips fewer than four leading spaces, so lines 9064-9076 (page 208) and 9291-9298 (page 213) render identically to the flush-left form here. Nothing that parses the file sees a difference. (5) The claim's supporting premise is also partly wrong. It cites page 208 as observing the convention, but page 209 - the DIRECT CONTINUATION of that very same list, items c) through e) of 8.8.1.4.4 at lines 9083-9099 - is likewise flush left. The indentation is lost across page boundaries throughout the transcription, which places this squarely in the 'page-break furniture / formatting' class rather than making page 211 an anomalous deviation from an otherwise-honored convention. Verdict: cosmetic whitespace inconsistency in the transcription, no content lost, no meaning changed - not a reportable discrepancy.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. The indentation difference is real but purely presentational: all of items a)-d) and their sub-expressions are transcribed verbatim and in order, the a)/b)/c)/d) vs 1)/2) enumerator series still scopes the nesting unambiguously, and three-space indentation is not semantic in Markdown anyway. The same flattening occurs at every page break in this transcription (e.g. page 209, the continuation of the identical list in 8.8.1.4.4), so it is page-break formatting furniture rather than a page-211-specific defect.
